title: DNS Terminology
summary: Gives current definitions for many terms used in DNS, which is specified in dozens of RFCs and whose terms have changed over the decades. It is Best Current Practice, and has been replaced by RFC 9499.

eli5.summary: Words about the internet phone book have changed over time. This is a dictionary of what they mean.

questions: what does authoritative server mean in dns
what is the difference between a recursive resolver and an authoritative server
what is an rrset in dns
what are the dnssec validation states
what does nodata mean in dns
subtitle: A single reference that gives the current meaning of the many terms used to describe the Domain Name System.

tldr.problem: The DNS is defined in dozens of RFCs, and some of its terms have shifted meaning since 1987, so people often use the same word to mean different things.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 8499 collects current definitions in one place, grouped by topic: names, response codes, transactions, resource records, servers and clients, zones, wildcards, registration and DNSSEC. Where a definition has changed, it gives a new stand-alone one and notes the difference.
tldr.outcome: It is a Best Current Practice that obsoleted RFC 7719 and updates RFC 2308, and it has itself been obsoleted by RFC 9499.

today: RFC 8499 is a Best Current Practice that has been obsoleted by RFC 9499, which is the current DNS terminology document. It replaced RFC 7719 and updates RFC 2308.

sections.title: Purpose and Scope
sections.content:
The DNS is a simple query-response protocol whose messages in both directions have the same format. It is defined in RFC 1034 and RFC 1035, and some of the terms from those documents mean something different now than they did in 1987. RFC 8499 is a collection of DNS-related terms, organized loosely by topic. Some terms were precisely defined in earlier RFCs, some loosely, and some not at all.

Where the consensus definition matches an RFC, that RFC is quoted. Where it has changed, the RFC is mentioned and a new stand-alone definition is given. The document says there is no single consistent definition of "the DNS", so it defines the global DNS and private DNS to deal with this. It is also not a tutorial: someone new to the DNS cannot learn it by reading from front to back, and skipping around, or using the index, may be the only way to get enough context.
sections.eli5: Grown-ups use many different words for the same parts of the internet's phone book. This document picks the meanings most people agree on and writes them down in one place.

sections.title: Names, Labels and Name Formats
sections.content:
A domain name is an ordered list of one or more labels. In the global DNS, each label is between 0 and 63 octets long, and a name has a maximum total length of 255 octets in wire format. In a fully-qualified name the last label has zero length and is called the root.

Names come in three formats. The wire format is a list of labels, each preceded by a length octet, ordered by decreasing distance from the root. The presentation format uses ASCII with a . between labels, and a fully-qualified name includes the root, as in example.tld.. The common display format is the same but usually leaves out the final dot.

The section also defines private DNS (names using the DNS protocol that do not rely on the global root zone), multicast DNS, FQDN, host name, top-level domain, subdomain, and the terms alias, canonical name and CNAME. It notes that a name's owner is called an alias, and that the owner of a CNAME record is not itself a canonical name.
sections.eli5: A web address is like a street address read backwards: each dot-separated piece is smaller or bigger than the next one. Each piece has a length limit, and the whole thing has one too.

sections.title: Response Codes, Queries and Records
sections.content:
Several response codes (RCODEs) from RFC 1035 have shorthand names: NOERROR, FORMERR, SERVFAIL, NXDOMAIN, NOTIMP and REFUSED. The document adds NODATA, a pseudo RCODE meaning the name is valid but has no records of the requested type. It is indicated by a NOERROR answer with no relevant answers. A negative response says an RRset does not exist or that the server cannot answer.

For transactions, the header of a DNS message is its first 12 octets. The QNAME is split into three meanings: original (the name in the question), effective (a name actually resolved, including names from a CNAME chain), and final (the last name in a CNAME chain). In general use QNAME means the original one. A referral is a response in which a server points the resolver to another place to ask. A downward referral is the normal kind, and an upward referral (a root referral) is not required for any correct resolution.

For records, an RRset is a set of resource records with the same owner name, class and type, and all must share one TTL. The TTL is the maximum time a record may be cached, with a maximum value of 2147483647. EDNS, defined in RFC 6891, lets clients and servers go beyond the original 512 octet message size limit.
sections.eli5: When you ask the phone book a question, the answer may be a result, a pointer to someone else to ask, or a note saying nothing like that exists. Each answer also says how long you may remember it before asking again.

sections.title: Servers, Resolvers and Clients
sections.content:
The terms "DNS server" and "name server" need context, because authoritative servers and recursive resolvers are both often called by those names. A resolver extracts information from name servers on behalf of clients. A stub resolver cannot do all resolution itself and depends on a recursive resolver. A recursive resolver acts in recursive mode, answering from its cache or querying other servers. A full-service resolver is a recursive resolver with a cache. In iterative resolution the client repeatedly sends non-recursive queries and follows referrals.

An authoritative server knows the content of a zone from local knowledge and answers with the AA flag set. A primary server is the source of zone transfers for secondary servers, using AXFR for the full zone or IXFR for changes only. Older "master" and "slave" wording is described as having shifted to "primary" and "secondary". Other terms include forwarder, open resolver, split DNS and views, anycast and instance, and privacy-enabling DNS server.

Resolvers need to know root servers to start. Priming is finding the list of root servers from configuration, often a root hints file.
sections.eli5: Some helpers only know the answer for their own street. Others will go and ask around for you and remember what they found. This part names each kind of helper and says what it does.

sections.title: Zones, Wildcards and Registration
sections.content:
A zone is a unit of authoritative information distributed to the name servers that serve it. Zones are separated by zone cuts, with a parent above and a child below. A delegation is created by adding an NS RRset in the parent zone for the child origin. The apex is the point of the zone's SOA and authoritative NS RRset. Glue records are address records needed when a name server's name is below the cut. A lame delegation is a delegated server that does not actually serve the zone. Names are called in-bailiwick or out-of-bailiwick depending on how they relate to the zone's origin, and the root zone has the zero-length label as its apex.

A wildcard is an RR whose owner name starts with the asterisk label, and it works as an instruction for synthesizing records. The section also defines closest encloser, next closer name and source of synthesis.

For registration, the registry runs a zone and decides what data goes into it, the registrant is the party a name is registered for, and the registrar is a go-between. EPP, WHOIS and RDAP are named, with RDAP meant as a replacement for WHOIS. The document calls the idea of a public suffix controversial in the DNS community.
sections.eli5: The big phone book is split into smaller books, each run by a different person. A pointer in the parent book tells you where the child book is, and a wildcard is a rule that answers for many names at once.

sections.title: DNSSEC Terms and States
sections.content:
Most DNSSEC terms come from RFC 4033, RFC 4034, RFC 4035 and RFC 5155. RFC 8499 highlights those that cause confusion. A signed zone has signed RRsets and properly constructed DNSKEY, RRSIG, NSEC and optionally DS records. Since RFC 6840, NSEC records are no longer required, because a signed zone may use NSEC3 instead. NSEC and NSEC3 both provide authenticated denial of existence; NSEC3 mitigates zone enumeration and supports opt-out.

Validation has three senses: checking signatures, checking responses such as denial of existence, and building an authentication chain from a trust anchor. A trust anchor is a configured DNSKEY or DS hash that a validating resolver uses as its starting point. Keys are described as key signing keys (KSK), zone signing keys (ZSK) or combined signing keys (CSK), and which one a key is depends on operational practice rather than protocol.

A validating resolver can place a response in one of four states: secure, insecure, bogus or indeterminate. The document says it does not reconcile the slightly different definitions in RFC 4033 and RFC 4035. Its own security section says the definitions do not change any security considerations for the DNS.
sections.eli5: DNSSEC is like a wax seal on the phone book's answers. A helper can check the seal back to a seal it already trusts. The answer is then trusted, untrusted, known to have no seal at all, or too unclear to say.

items.label: No error condition
items.desc: The query was processed without error.

items.label: Format error
items.desc: The name server was unable to interpret the query.

items.label: Server failure
items.desc: The server could not process the query due to a problem with the server.

items.label: Name error
items.desc: The domain name referenced in the query does not exist.

items.label: Not implemented
items.desc: The server does not support the requested kind of query.

items.label: Refused
items.desc: The server refuses the operation for policy reasons.

items.label: Pseudo RCODE
items.desc: The name is valid but has no records of the given type.

viz.caption: FOUR DNSSEC VALIDATION STATES (RFC 8499, from RFC 4033)

items.label: Verified
items.desc: Trust anchor and chain of trust exist, and all signatures verify.

items.label: Provably unsigned
items.desc: A chain of trust exists down to signed proof that no DS record exists.

items.label: Fails validation
items.desc: A secure delegation says data is signed, but the response does not validate.

items.label: No trust anchor
items.desc: No trust anchor indicates this part of the tree is secure; this is the default mode.
